opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find appealing about systems like AlphaFold is that they point to a path where AI gives us enormous benefits without many of the risks we worry about most with general-purpose, agentic systems.

AlphaFold is extraordinarily capable within its domain. It solved a fifty-year grand challenge in biology, predicting protein structures, and it's now used by millions of researchers around the world. But it's narrow. It isn't trying to pursue goals in the world, it isn't acting autonomously, and it isn't substituting for people. It's a tool that makes human scientists dramatically more productive. It complements human capability rather than replacing it.

That matters for a few reasons. First, on safety: a system like that has a much smaller attack surface for things going wrong. It's hard to see how a protein structure predictor develops misaligned goals or tries to evade oversight. The risks are real but more bounded and easier to reason about, like misuse in biology, and we can govern those more targeted risks more directly.

Second, on the social and economic side: complementary systems tend to preserve human agency and human economic relevance. If AI mostly amplifies what people can do, the gains are more likely to be broadly shared, and we're less likely to end up in a world where human labor and human judgment get displaced wholesale. Much of my worry about the long-run trajectory is about the gradual disempowerment of humans, even without any dramatic catastrophe, and complementary AI pushes the other way.

Third, it's a reminder that we have some choice about which direction the technology goes. There's a tendency to treat the march toward general, autonomous agents as inevitable, and competitive pressures do push hard in that direction, because general systems are economically attractive. But AlphaFold shows you can get transformative, Nobel Prize-level scientific value from targeted systems. If we can direct more investment, talent, and prestige toward those kinds of applications, in science, medicine, materials, and climate, we might capture much of the upside of AI while buying time to figure out how to safely handle more general systems.

I wouldn't claim it's a complete strategy. The pull toward generality is strong, and narrow systems increasingly get built on top of general foundation models anyway. But as part of the portfolio, and as a vision of what beneficial AI can look like, I find it genuinely hopeful.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold makes human scientists dramatically more productive and mentions science and medicine, but it does not state that this enables research productivity that would otherwise be impossible.

r002.rationale: The response recommends directing more investment, talent, and prestige toward targeted systems like AlphaFold as a way to achieve beneficial AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think what's appealing about AlphaFold, and systems like it, is that it shows you a path to getting an enormous amount of value out of AI without needing to build something that is itself an agent pursuing open-ended goals in the world. AlphaFold is a tool. It takes a well-specified problem, predicting the three-dimensional structure of a protein from its amino acid sequence, and it solves that problem at a level that essentially leapfrogged decades of work. And then it hands the answer back to a human scientist who decides what to do with it.

So it's complementary in a few senses. It complements human researchers rather than substituting for them: biologists are still asking the questions, designing the experiments, interpreting the results. It fits into existing institutions, labs, universities, pharma companies, without demanding that those institutions reorganize themselves around it. And crucially, the system has no reason, and really no capacity, to develop its own agenda. There's no planning horizon, no persistent goals, no resource acquisition. The failure modes are mostly the ordinary ones of a scientific instrument, it might be wrong, people might over-trust it, rather than the more exotic failure modes we worry about with highly agentic systems.

I think that matters because when people talk about transformative AI, the mental image is often a single very general agent that goes off and does things. But a lot of the benefit we actually want, in medicine, in materials science, in energy, could in principle come from a portfolio of narrower, superhuman tools that are each deeply embedded in a human workflow. If you can capture a large fraction of the upside that way, you buy time, and you make the governance problem more tractable, because you're governing tools and the humans who use them, which we have a lot of experience doing, rather than trying to govern autonomous actors.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. The economic and competitive incentives push toward generality and autonomy, because that's where you get the most leverage. And "narrow" is a slippery notion; capabilities developed for one tool often transfer. So I don't think complementary systems are a complete answer. But as a design philosophy, and as a demonstration of what's possible, I find AlphaFold really encouraging. It's an existence proof that "superhuman" and "dangerous" don't have to travel together.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold delivers enormous value and leapfrogged decades of work, but it does not state that this productivity would otherwise be impossible.

r002.rationale: The response calls complementary systems an encouraging design philosophy and describes building a portfolio of narrower tools as a way to capture benefits.

astra-6.text:
What I find appealing is that they expand what humans can do. AlphaFold helps us understand protein structures, and that gives scientists a powerful tool for making further discoveries. It’s a way for AI to contribute to science without having to replace the scientist or take over the whole process of research.

And I think that’s a promising direction to encourage: systems that complement human expertise, that help us understand the world and make better decisions. You can get enormous benefits from a system that’s very capable at a particular task without giving it broad autonomy or the ability to pursue goals in the world.

That doesn’t mean there are no risks. But it suggests that we should pay attention to what kinds of AI we’re building, alongside how capable they are. There may be a lot of value in directing progress toward tools that strengthen human capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold helps scientists understand protein structures and make further discoveries, but it does not state that this enables medical or health research productivity that would otherwise be impossible.

r002.rationale: The response calls complementary systems a promising direction to encourage and says progress should be directed toward tools that strengthen human capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find appealing is that they expand what we can do in a way that complements human effort. AlphaFold helps us understand protein structures, and that can enable scientists to make progress on a whole range of problems. It’s a capability that other people can build on.

That’s a useful lens for thinking about which kinds of AI we want to develop. Are we building systems that help people discover things, make better decisions, and solve shared problems? Or are we primarily making people better at competing with one another? Those can both be commercially valuable, but their social consequences can be quite different.

I’d like us to put more effort into AI that expands the space of possibilities for everyone—scientific tools are a good example—rather than simply intensifying competition over what already exists.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold helps scientists understand protein structures and advance various problems, but it does not state that this enables otherwise impossible productivity in medical or health research.

r002.rationale: It explicitly favors putting more effort into AI that expands possibilities for everyone, citing scientific tools such as AlphaFold as an example.
